summary.text: Naive Bayes classifiers are a family of probabilistic classifiers that assume the features are conditionally independent, given the target class.
The assumption is highly unrealistic, which is where the name comes from, yet these classifiers have worked quite well in many complex real-world situations.
They are highly scalable and need only a small amount of training data to estimate their parameters.

facts.label: Core assumption
facts.value: Each feature is independent of the others, given the class

items.prompt: A fruit is red, round and about 10 cm across. How does a naive Bayes classifier treat these three clues when deciding if it is an apple?

options.label: It lets each clue contribute on its own
It looks only at the colour
It checks how the clues are correlated
It averages the clues into one number

items.explain: It considers each feature to contribute independently to the probability that the fruit is an apple, regardless of any correlations between them.

items.prompt: What gives the naive Bayes classifier its name?

options.label: Its inventor was a beginner
Its results are always poor
It needs no training data whatsoever
Its independence assumption is highly unrealistic

items.explain: The highly unrealistic assumption that features are independent, called the naive independence assumption, gives the classifier its name.

items.prompt: You have only a small amount of labelled training data. Why might naive Bayes still be a sensible option?

options.label: It cannot make mistakes with little data
It needs only a small amount to estimate its parameters
It makes up extra data to fill the gap
It always beats every other classifier

items.explain: An advantage of naive Bayes is that it only requires a small amount of training data to estimate the parameters needed for classification.

items.prompt: A naive Bayes model announces it is 99.9% sure about many answers, yet it is often wrong. Which known weakness fits?

options.label: It cannot handle more than two classes
It always refuses to give a probability
It often gives wildly overconfident probabilities
It ignores the class labels

items.explain: Naive Bayes models often produce wildly overconfident probabilities, so they are generally worse than more advanced models at quantifying uncertainty.

items.prompt: A statistician fits a naive Bayes model using maximum likelihood and no Bayesian methods at all. Is that allowed?

options.label: Yes, it can be fit with frequentist methods too
No, it must be fit with Bayesian methods
No, maximum likelihood cannot be used here
Yes, but only for continuous data

items.explain: Despite using Bayes' theorem in its decision rule, naive Bayes is not necessarily a Bayesian method, and it can be fit with either Bayesian or frequentist methods.

items.prompt: How is maximum-likelihood training of a naive Bayes model typically done?

options.label: By repeating a long, costly iterative approximation
By counting observations in each group with a closed-form expression
By asking an expert to set each parameter by hand
By trying every possible class for every feature

items.explain: It can be done by evaluating a closed-form expression, simply by counting observations in each group, rather than the expensive iterative approximation algorithms most other models need.
